title: Croesus on the Pyre Calls Out Solon's Name
text:
Croesus, king of Lydia, was famous for his wealth. Herodotus says that years earlier the Athenian lawgiver Solon had visited him and refused to call him the happiest of men, saying no one should be called happy until his life had ended well.

Around 546 BC the Persian king Cyrus captured Croesus's capital, Sardis. According to Herodotus, Cyrus had a great pyre built and placed Croesus on it in chains with fourteen Lydian boys. Standing there, Croesus remembered Solon's words and groaned his name three times.

Cyrus had interpreters ask him whom he was calling. At first Croesus would not answer. Then he told the story of Solon's visit. Cyrus, Herodotus says, reflected that he too was a man, about to burn alive another man who had once been as fortunate as himself, and that nothing human is secure. He ordered the fire put out, but it had taken hold. Croesus prayed to Apollo, and a sudden storm quenched the flames.

Cyrus freed him and kept him as an adviser. Croesus's first counsel was to stop the soldiers plundering Sardis, since it was now Cyrus's own city they were looting.
lesson: When you have the upper hand, remember that fortune turns. Treating the defeated as you would want to be treated is both decent and wise.
source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 1, chapters 29 to 33 and 86 to 88
caveat: Solon's visit is chronologically unlikely, and other ancient sources give different accounts of Croesus's fate.
